title: Crossed treble
subtitle: Two tall stitches that cross in an X over a shared space
excerpt: The crossed treble is a decorative pair: two tall stitches worked so the second crosses in front of the first, making a small X. It gives an open, latticed fabric and a textured surface, and it is the basis of many Victorian openwork patterns.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passage on crossed trebles (Fig. 421). Public domain via Project Gutenberg. UK and US stitch-name equivalences cross-checked against the Craft Yarn Council standard terms.

glossaryTerms.definition: A decorative pair of tall stitches worked so the second crosses over the first, leaving a small X with an open space behind it. Built from trebles or double trebles depending on the pattern.
The United States name for crossed trebles, since the US calls a UK treble a double crochet. The crossing method is identical; only the stitch name underneath changes.
Wrapping the working yarn over the hook from back to front before working a stitch. Each tall stitch in a crossed pair begins with at least one wrap.

content.text: is a pair of tall stitches that lean across one another to make a small X over an open space. You skip a stitch, work a tall post, then reach back and work a second post over the top of the first so they cross. The result is a latticed, textured fabric with little windows of light through it. content.text: Begin with one working loop on the hook. This version crosses two trebles; for taller crosses, swap in double trebles and add a wrap of
Skip the next stitch and work a treble into the stitch after it.
Wrap the yarn over the hook once, then carry the hook back in front of that treble.
Work a second treble into the stitch you skipped, drawing the post across the front of the first. The two stitches now cross.
Work one chain to lock the crossing in place before moving to the next pair.
Keep the crossing post a touch looser than usual, so it reaches over the first without puckering the fabric.

Crossed trebles make textured, open panels for shawls, table linens, and the bodies of Victorian-style edgings. Rows of them give a fabric that reads as a fine lattice, more interesting than plain trebles but still quick to work. They are good where you want decoration in the stitch itself rather than in a separate motif.

Crossing double trebles instead of trebles gives a taller, more open X for deeper lace. Working the cross over three stitches rather than two makes a wider, more slanted lattice. The plain treble is the building block underneath; once you can cross two trebles cleanly, the taller versions follow the same move.
Difficulty: intermediate. The stitches themselves are familiar; the new skill is reaching back to cross without twisting the fabric.
